---
title: "A4 — Water, ions and excretion"
---

## Why does living in water not solve water balance?

A freshwater fish is surrounded by water yet must control water entry and
replace ions. A marine bony fish faces the opposite tendencies: it loses water
and gains salts. A terrestrial mammal can conserve water, but eliminating
nitrogen and dissipating heat still create costs. This unit connects the
physical tendencies of water and solutes with epithelial transport, excretory
organs and whole-animal regulation.

You should become able to predict osmotic tendencies, distinguish osmotic
concentration from tonicity, compare aquatic strategies, trace a nephron,
calculate excretion from filtration/reabsorption/secretion, and explain how
water and nitrogen balance interact. Use the [slides](lec.qmd),
[exercises](exercise.qmd) and [quiz](quiz.qmd).

## Begin with a boundary and a permeability

Water moves across a selectively permeable membrane in response to differences
in water chemical potential. In an elementary osmotic comparison at equal
pressure, the side containing more effectively retained solute tends to draw
water from the other side. State which boundary is being considered: the skin,
gill, intestinal wall, capillary wall and cell membrane are not interchangeable.
Water entry into the animal and water entry into one of its cells are different
questions.

**Osmolarity** counts osmotically active particles per litre of solution, often
in osmoles L⁻¹ or milliosmoles L⁻¹. For an ideal teaching example, 0.10 mol L⁻¹
glucose contributes about 0.10 Osm L⁻¹, while 0.10 mol L⁻¹ NaCl contributes
about 0.20 Osm L⁻¹ if treated as fully dissociated. Real solutions need not
behave ideally. These particle counts are useful because osmosis depends on
particle concentration, not simply the mass of dissolved material.

**Tonicity** predicts sustained effects on cell volume and depends on solutes
that do not readily equilibrate across the relevant membrane. Two solutions
with equal total osmolarity need not have the same effect if their solutes
cross a membrane differently. Avoid treating every dissolved molecule as a
permanently trapped osmotic particle. Hydrostatic pressure also matters:
movement need not continue until solute concentrations are equal if an opposing
pressure develops. The supporting reading introduces
[osmotic balance](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/41-1-osmoregulation-and-osmotic-balance).

## A permeable surface creates a transport problem

Respiratory surfaces must exchange gases, but permeability creates opportunities
for water and ions to move as well. An animal cannot always make its surface
perfectly impermeable while preserving other functions. It can instead alter
surface properties, drink or stop drinking, move ions actively, and change urine
volume and composition.

A typical freshwater teleost has body fluids more concentrated than the
surrounding water. Water tends to enter and ions tend to be lost. It produces
relatively large volumes of dilute urine and obtains ions through specialised
transport processes and food. A typical marine teleost has body fluids less
concentrated than seawater. It drinks seawater, absorbs water through the gut
and eliminates excess salts through gill and renal processes. The two fish
therefore use related epithelia to address different net challenges.

These are broad teleost examples, not descriptions of every fish. Marine
elasmobranchs, such as sharks, retain organic osmolytes including urea and
have a different strategy. Many marine invertebrates have total internal
osmotic concentrations near those of their environment, yet may still regulate
particular ions. An **osmoconformer** need not have every internal solute
identical to seawater, and an **osmoregulator** need not maintain an absolutely
unchanging internal concentration at every salinity. State the species and
conditions before generalising.

## Epithelia can move material against a tendency

An epithelial transport cell has different membrane domains facing different
fluids. ATP-driven pumps establish ion gradients. Other proteins couple a
solute's movement to those gradients; channels allow selected ions to move
down electrochemical gradients. Water can follow osmotic gradients through
membranes and water channels. The epithelium and its cell junctions determine
which routes are available.

This polarity makes directional transport possible. A list of pumps without
their locations does not explain net movement from the environment to blood.
Draw both boundaries of a cell and show how each protein contributes to an
overall route. Energy expenditure can occur at one step while another step
is passive. “Water is actively pumped by the kidney” is therefore a poor
description of water following gradients produced by solute transport.

## The nephron separates filtration from selective recovery

In a mammalian kidney, blood enters a glomerular capillary network. Filtration
produces fluid in the nephron that normally contains water and many small
solutes but few cells and little large plasma protein. A filtered molecule
has left the blood and entered the tubular lumen; it has not necessarily
left the body. Much of that filtered material is subsequently returned to blood.

**Reabsorption** moves material from tubular fluid towards blood.
**Secretion** moves material from blood/interstitium towards tubular fluid.
**Excretion** is the amount finally leaving in urine. For a stated substance
and time interval, use the accounting relation:

$$\text{excretion}=\text{filtered load}-\text{reabsorption}+\text{secretion}.$$

For example, a filtered load of 100 arbitrary amount units min⁻¹, reabsorption
of 98 and secretion of 1 gives excretion of 3 units min⁻¹. Keep amount per
time distinct from concentration. If urine concentration is 2 mmol L⁻¹ and
urine flow is 0.001 L min⁻¹, excretion is 0.002 mmol min⁻¹. Concentrated urine
does not alone establish a large total amount excreted.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  B[Blood in glomerular capillaries] -->|Filtration| F[Fluid in nephron lumen]
  F --> T[Proximal tubule → loop → distal tubule]
  T --> C[Collecting duct]
  C --> U[Urine leaving kidney]
  T -->|Reabsorption| R[Blood around tubule]
  R -->|Secretion| T
```

The diagram is an original functional sketch; it does not show physical scale
or every nephron connection. The collecting duct receives fluid from multiple
nephrons. Use it to keep transport direction explicit while reading the account
of [kidneys and osmoregulatory organs](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/41-2-the-kidneys-and-osmoregulatory-organs).

## How can urine become more concentrated than plasma?

Water reabsorption requires an osmotic driving force and a water-permeable
route. In the mammalian kidney, specialised loop segments differ in water
permeability and solute transport. Their arrangement, together with other
transport and urea-handling processes, helps establish a medullary osmotic
gradient. Blood vessels serving the medulla help preserve this organisation
while supplying tissue. The collecting duct passes through that gradient.

Antidiuretic hormone, ADH or vasopressin, can increase collecting-duct water
permeability. More water then leaves the tubular fluid when an appropriate
gradient exists, reducing urine volume and increasing its concentration.
The hormone does not manufacture water or simply “make the kidney filter less”.
The full concentrating mechanism is more complex than one salt pump or one
hairpin loop. Here, be able to explain differential permeability, gradient,
water recovery and hormonal control before memorising segment names.

When osmotic concentration of body fluids rises, sensing and control processes
can increase ADH release and promote drinking. When the disturbance is corrected,
feedback reduces the response. Blood-volume/pressure signals can also influence
water conservation; it is not a one-input switch. Compare this loop with A1's
temperature example. The reading on
[hormonal regulation](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/37-3-regulation-of-body-processes)
provides a complementary account.

## Nitrogen disposal is part of the water budget

Breaking down amino acids creates nitrogen-containing waste. Ammonia can be
released with relatively little conversion, but its handling requires attention
to toxicity, concentration and removal. Urea costs energy to synthesise but
can be retained or excreted at concentrations suitable for many animals.
Uric acid can be eliminated with little water in a semi-solid form, though
its production also has costs. No product is universally best: water availability,
life stage, habitat and other physiological demands matter.

Terrestrial insects use Malpighian tubules and hindgut processes rather than
mammalian nephrons. Many annelids and other invertebrates use different tubular
excretory arrangements. Compare the tasks—removing waste, controlling ions,
recovering water—before comparing anatomical names. Egestion of undigested
food remains different from excretion of metabolically produced nitrogen.

## Read structure and behaviour together

A kidney section may contain round tubule profiles, glomeruli and blood
vessels, but section angle can change apparent shape. Look for a capillary
tuft within a surrounding space when identifying a renal corpuscle; look
for epithelial organisation around a lumen in tubules. These descriptions
are preparation for the real slide set, not proof that a particular specimen
is available. Finally, connect anatomy to the environment: a water-saving
animal may also change behaviour, diet, ventilation and heat exchange.
Continue to [integration, movement and reproduction](../integration/index.qmd).
